Separate accounts per surface

Customers, vendors and admins each get their own account table, session table and cookie. A cookie from one surface opens nothing on another.

 Postgres stays the only store No login changes for customers Two questions below

Today one users table and one cookie serve all three apps, so a role check is the only thing between a vendor session and an admin route.

  • One users table with a role column
  • One sessions table, one cookie for every app
  • Each route checks the role after loading the user
    •
  • customer_accounts, vendor_accounts, admin_accounts
  • A session table and a cookie per surface
  • Each route reads only its own cookie — the wrong one is simply not seen

    • s3 · vendor 12
     reads ub_admin_session

    Signing in writes one row to vendor_sessions and sets one cookie: ub_vendor_session.

    The vendor guard looks the cookie up in its own table and finds vendor 42.

    The admin guard never reads the vendor cookie, so it sees no session at all: 401, even though vendor 42 is staff.

    Signing out deletes that one row. Sessions on the shop or the admin app are untouched.

         Two logins, one per surface

    Matches the tables exactly. Staff sign in twice, which is also the audit trail we want.

     One login, linked accounts

    Friendlier, but brings back a shared identity — the coupling this plan removes.

    Each users row is copied to the table for its role, and an id map records the old id next to the new one, so foreign keys can follow.

    • 1 · ana · customer
    • 2 · bo · vendor
    • 3 · cy · admin
    • e1 · by user 2

    The first PR only adds tables. Nothing reads them yet, so it is safe to ship alone.

    Ana lands in customer_accounts, and the map remembers where user 1 went.

    Same for every role. The copy is idempotent: rerunning it skips users already in the map.

    Every “who did this” column is rewritten through the map: user 2 becomes vendor v1.

    The last PR, one release after nothing reads them: drop users and the map.

    A column like order_events.changed_by_user_id could point at any user. It becomes two nullable foreign keys, and a check makes sure exactly one is set. Try it:

    order_events e1

    Click a column to set or clear it. The check is num_nonnulls(changed_by_vendor_id, changed_by_admin_id) = 1.

     alter table order_events add column changed_by_vendor_id bigint references vendor_accounts (id), add column changed_by_admin_id bigint references admin_accounts (id), add constraint order_events_one_actor check (num_nonnulls(changed_by_vendor_id, changed_by_admin_id) = 1);

    Four pull requests, each safe to deploy and roll back on its own.

    New account, session and map tables; the copy job; the two-FK columns with their check. Old tables untouched.

    Three guards, three cookies. Each route group reads only its own cookie and session table.

    Shop, vendor panel and admin sign in against their own endpoints. Old sessions expire naturally.

    Drop users, sessions, the map and the old *_user_id columns.

         One full release

    Long enough for every old session to expire; the logs prove nothing reads users.

     Two weeks of quiet logs

    Safer for a slow-moving mobile app, but the map lives longer.
    • Everyone is signed out once when PR 3 ships — announce it to vendors the day before.
    • A missed foreign key keeps pointing at users; PR 4 fails loudly rather than silently, because the drop is blocked by it.
